stemMd: A cyclist rides round a corner in a Turin street. Just before the corner her velocity is 6 m/s due east. Exactly 2 s later, just after the corner, it is 8 m/s due north. What is the magnitude of her average acceleration during these 2 s?
explanationMd:
Acceleration is a vector: $\vec a = \Delta\vec v/\Delta t$, where $\Delta\vec v$ is the final velocity minus the initial velocity. What matters is the change of direction as well as the change of speed.

**The velocity change.** Subtracting an eastward 6 m/s is the same as adding a westward 6 m/s. So $\Delta\vec v$ has a component of 6 m/s to the west and a component of 8 m/s to the north. These are at right angles, so
$$|\Delta\vec v| = \sqrt{6^{2}+8^{2}} = 10\ \text{m/s}.$$

**Divide by the time.** $|\vec a| = 10/2 = 5\ \text{m/s}^2$.

**Check.** By the triangle inequality the size of the velocity change must lie between the difference of the speeds (8 - 6 = 2 m/s) and their sum (14 m/s). Dividing by 2 s, the acceleration must lie between 1 and 7 m/s². The value 5 is inside that range, and the right-angle case gives exactly the 6-8-10 triangle.

distractorRationale.b: Subtracts the speeds, (8 - 6) ÷ 2 = 1, as if the cyclist stayed on one straight line. The two velocities point in perpendicular directions, so the velocity change is not 2 m/s.
distractorRationale.e: Adds the two speeds, (6 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7, treating perpendicular vectors as if they pointed the same way. Magnitudes add only for parallel vectors.
distractorRationale.d: Finds the size of the velocity change correctly (10 m/s) but does not divide by the 2 s. That is a change of velocity, not an acceleration.
distractorRationale.c: Adds the two speeds (6 + 8 = 14) and does not divide by the time, so it makes both the vector-addition error and the missing-division error.

accessibilityText: A vector question. A cyclist has velocity 6 metres per second due east just before a corner, and 2 seconds later 8 metres per second due north. The magnitude of her average acceleration over those 2 seconds is wanted. The choices are 1, 5, 7, 10 and 14 metres per second squared.

provenance.notes: Original item. Uses the 6-8-10 right triangle so the arithmetic is exact by hand. Wrong choices: subtracting speeds, adding speeds, forgetting the division by time, and both errors together.

independentSolve.workingNotes: Δv = (-6, 8), so |Δv| = 10 m/s; average acceleration = 10/2 = 5 m/s^2. 1 m/s^2 uses only the change in speed, 7 comes from adding the speeds, and 10 forgets to divide by the time. [A second, separate blind solve (blind-reviewer-wave6-tili-phys-tech-run9) reached the same answer: Delta v = (-6, 8), magnitude 10 m/s; over 2 s gives 5 m/s^2. 1 is (8-6)/2, 7 is (6+8)/2, 10 forgets dividing by time, 14 is sum of speeds.]
